title: Retina Anatomy: Rods, Cones & Ten Neural Layers | Guide
description: Understand retina anatomy at the cellular level, tracing light across all ten retinal layers, rod and cone photoreceptors, bipolar relays, and optic axons.
h1: Retina Microanatomy: Photoreceptors, Ten Neural Layers and Fovea
blurb: How light traverses ten transparent neural layers to trigger rod and cone phototransduction, bipolar-to-ganglion processing, and high-acuity foveal vision.
lead: The human retina is an outpost of the central nervous system where incoming photons pass through transparent interneurons before striking rods and cones at the back. In this illustrated guide to retina neural layers anatomy, we examine 20 documented structures—including internal limiting membrane, nerve fiber layer, ganglion cell layer, inner plexiform layer—linking regional topography, tissue architecture, physiological mechanisms, and clinical reasoning.
overview: The human retina is an outpost of the central nervous system where incoming photons pass through transparent interneurons before striking rods and cones at the back. Light traverses inner retinal layers before reaching rods and cones against retinal pigment epithelium (RPE). Neural signaling runs the opposite direction: photoreceptors → bipolar cells → ganglion cells → optic nerve. Horizontal and amacrine cells modify lateral signaling. The foveal center has dense cones and displaced inner layers for acuity, while the optic disc has no photoreceptors. Inner retina is supported mainly by central retinal circulation; photoreceptors and RPE depend strongly on the choriocapillaris. Within the human body, the retina · neural microanatomy (Retina neurosensorialis · epithelium pigmentosum) is situated in inner posterior globe; photoreceptors interface with pigment epithelium and choroid, receives arterial perfusion via inner retina: central retinal artery; outer retina: choriocapillaris, and is innervated by ganglion cell axons → optic nerve II; autonomic supply regulates ocular vessels.

Structurally, the internal limiting membrane (Membrana limitans interna) comprises müller-cell endfeet make retinal inner boundary against vitreous. Physiologically, the internal limiting membrane supports vitreoretinal interface. Structurally, the nerve fiber layer (Stratum neurofibrarum) comprises unmyelinated ganglion axons converge toward optic disc. Physiologically, the nerve fiber layer conducts output to optic nerve. Structurally, the ganglion cell layer (Stratum ganglionare) comprises retinal ganglion somata whose axons become optic nerve. Physiologically, the ganglion cell layer governs final retinal output neurons. Structurally, the inner plexiform layer (Stratum plexiforme internum) comprises synapses among bipolar, amacrine and ganglion processes. Physiologically, the inner plexiform layer processes contrast and temporal information. Structurally, the inner nuclear layer (Stratum nucleare internum) comprises bipolar, horizontal, amacrine and Müller cell bodies. Physiologically, the inner nuclear layer relays and modulates photoreceptor signals. Structurally, the outer plexiform layer (Stratum plexiforme externum) comprises photoreceptor terminals synapse with bipolar and horizontal cells. Physiologically, the outer plexiform layer governs first central synaptic relay for light signals.

Clinically, regarding the internal limiting membrane, epiretinal traction can distort macula. From a diagnostic standpoint, in the nerve fiber layer, glaucoma thins nerve fiber layer. In clinical pathology involving the ganglion cell layer, ganglion-cell loss contributes to glaucomatous vision loss. Medical evaluation of the inner plexiform layer also notes that layer distortion can accompany retinal edema.

questions.question: Where are rods and cones located in the retina?
questions.answer: Photoreceptors lie in the outer neural retina next to retinal pigment epithelium, even though incoming light first passes through more internal layers. Structurally, the retinal pigment epithelium (Epithelium pigmentosum retinae) comprises pigmented monolayer adjacent to photoreceptors and Bruch membrane. Physiologically, the retinal pigment epithelium governs recycles visual pigment, phagocytoses shed discs and forms outer blood–retinal barrier.

questions.question: What is the difference between rods and cones?
questions.answer: Rods are especially sensitive in low light; cones support high-acuity and color vision, particularly near the fovea. Structurally, the cones (Coni) comprises color- and acuity-sensitive photoreceptors concentrated at fovea. Physiologically, the cones governs high-resolution daylight and color vision.

questions.question: What are the photoreceptor segments?
questions.answer: Rod and cone inner/outer segments facing RPE. Functionally, it governs capture photons and start phototransduction. In clinical pathology involving the photoreceptor segments, outer-segment injury impairs vision despite intact inner retina.

questions.question: Where is the retinal pigment epithelium located?
questions.answer: Pigmented monolayer adjacent to photoreceptors and Bruch membrane. Functionally, it governs recycles visual pigment, phagocytoses shed discs and forms outer blood–retinal barrier. Structurally, the external limiting membrane (Membrana limitans externa) comprises adherens junction belt between Müller cells and photoreceptors. Physiologically, the external limiting membrane provides organized retinal scaffold.

questions.question: What is the function of the fovea centralis?
questions.answer: Functionally, it governs peak spatial acuity. Small central pit with closely spaced cones and displaced inner layers. Clinically, regarding the fovea centralis, foveal injury causes major central visual impairment.
